Content covers: the resolution of a nine-versus-ten sanctification count discrepancy via the tenth sanctification performed at the day's final undressing from sacred to ordinary garments, contrasted with Rabbi Meir's view that this final change requires no sanctification at all since he never dons sacred garments again (l01); the beraita establishing that Aaron's entry to the Tent of Meeting to remove the ladle and fire-pan is the sole exception to the passage's otherwise strict chronological ordering, with Rashi's extended demonstration of what the 'correct' order would have been and why the verse instead groups the ladle-removal with the inner services (l03); Rav Chisda's transmitted tradition of five immersions and ten sanctifications, and his own derivation that a strict chronological reading of the verses yields only three immersions and six sanctifications, requiring three additional inferred breaks (before the ram-offerings, before the ladle-removal, and before the afternoon daily-offering) to reach five, each with its own garment-color pattern (l07); the verse's phrase 'and he shall don his garments' establishing that every change between an inner and outer service requires immersion, with Rashi's forward cross-reference to the mishna's own later count of five distinct services (l10); Rebbi's own derivation from the phrase 'a sacred linen tunic he shall wear, and bathe in water' governing the transition from the daily-offering to the day's own inner service, and the three superfluous words in 'they are sacred garments' that ground a further exposition (l16); the note that this five-service count works for both Rebbi's and Rabbi Yehuda's readings, and Rebbi's derivation of the immersions themselves from the bathing verse tied to the white garments, leaving the golden-garment verse available for Rabbi Yehuda's own derivation of the two sanctifications bracketing each undressing and dressing (l27); Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's kal vachomer argument that sanctification should be required wherever immersion is required, since immersion applies even outside Yom Kippur's special garment changes (l29); and the counter-question of whether sanctification might be limited to a single instance per immersion (as elsewhere), answered by the verse 'and he shall remove the linen garments which he wore,' whose superfluous 'which he wore' teaches that undressing itself is juxtaposed to dressing and thus also requires sanctification, with Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's own alternate reading reserving that verse for immersion's own requirement to change into golden garments, following Rabbi Yehuda (l31).
